content: 1. A retrospective cohort study by Duffus WA et al. (2009) revealed that the absence of routine HIV screening in South Carolina correctional facilities led to missed opportunities for early HIV diagnosis among inmates. Implementing routine screening and testing in prisons is essential to facilitate early detection of HIV. 2. Jafa K et al. (2009) demonstrated that delayed HIV diagnosis among prison inmates was due to insufficient testing in correctional facilities. The study highlighted the critical importance of timely diagnosis and appropriate treatment, especially given the high proportion of seroconverters infected with drug-resistant HIV strains. 3. Javanbakht M et al. (2007) reported that prevention programs in the MSM (men who have sex with men) unit included individual-level HIV education, condom distribution, and HIV/STI counseling. Screening efforts revealed a high prevalence of STIs and HIV among this population. 4. Beckwith CG et al. (2010) found that only 28% of participants in a conventional cohort received their HIV test results, compared to 100% in a rapid testing cohort. Rapid testing significantly improved the likelihood of inmates receiving their test results. 5. Macgowan R et al. (2009) demonstrated that rapid HIV testing identified a substantial number of previously undiagnosed cases and significantly increased the number of prisoners receiving their results in a timely manner. 6. Motshabi LC et al. (2011) found that while most participants were knowledgeable about HIV transmission, barriers to testing and counseling included stigma, discrimination, mistrust of healthcare professionals, poor attitudes of healthcare staff, and lack of awareness about voluntary counseling and testing (VCT) services. Programs addressing stigma and discrimination among healthcare workers are recommended. 7. De Voux A et al. (2012) reported that the EnhanceLink demonstration project showed that HIV testing in jails could lead to early diagnosis of new HIV infections. Rapid turnover of inmates did not hinder jail-based HIV screening, but linkage to care post-release was emphasized as most inmates did not initiate care while detained. 8. Beckwith CG et al. (2011) highlighted positive experiences with rapid HIV testing among staff and key informants. Rapid testing was preferred over conventional methods, as it increased prisoner compliance and reduced staff workload. Immediate access to test results was seen as a major advantage, particularly in high-turnover settings. 9. Strick LB et al. (2011) showed that changing testing procedures from opt-in to opt-out in Washington State jails increased testing rates among inmates from 5% to 72% and then to 90%. Opt-out testing proved to be the most effective method for case detection. 10. Tartaro C et al. (2012) noted that as part of the testing process, inmates were assured of free medical care during their jail stay and outpatient treatment post-release for those without health insurance. Rapid testing increased the number of inmates receiving test results before discharge, with many receiving their first HIV test in jail. 11. Tuli K et al. (2009) described HIV and syphilis screening and condom distribution programs in the MSM unit of the Los Angeles County jail. Modeling suggested that these interventions could prevent numerous sexually transmitted infections at low cost and save costs in scenarios where inmates continued sexual activity similar to outside jail. 12. A 2007 review by UNODC, UNAIDS, and WHO emphasized the need for comprehensive HIV prevention programs in prisons, including education, condom provision, needle and syringe programs, drug dependence treatment, and access to antiretroviral therapy (ART). Evidence showed that ART significantly reduced mortality due to HIV/AIDS in countries where it was accessible, including among incarcerated individuals. 13. Roberson DW et al. (2009) identified barriers to ART adherence in prisons, such as lack of confidentiality, stigma, limited access to medication, and strained relationships with prison health staff. ART programs should include inmate input, protect medical information, and improve provider-inmate relationships while addressing stigma. 14. Fontana L et al. (2007) reported a lack of continuity of care between prison and community settings during the release period. Improved discharge models and collaboration between prison systems and community healthcare providers are necessary to retain patients in care. 15. Small W et al. (2009) noted delays in obtaining HIV care and treatment in Canadian prisons. Poor relationships between prison health staff and inmates, high levels of stigma, and challenges in ensuring continuity of treatment post-release were identified as significant barriers. 16. Shalihu N et al. (2014) identified barriers to ART adherence in Namibian prisons, including insufficient privacy, stigma, lack of adherence support, poor nutrition, discrimination by prison staff, and lack of information about HIV transmission and care. 17. Wohl DA et al. (2011) found that an intensive case management intervention during incarceration and post-release was as effective as comprehensive pre-release discharge planning in ensuring access to medical care for HIV-infected individuals. 18. Nunn A et al. (2010) reported that the COMPASS program, an intensive case-management initiative, improved linkage to HIV care and other services for HIV-positive jail inmates in Rhode Island. Participants noted benefits such as preventing drug relapse and securing housing and mental health care post-release. 19. Catz SL et al. (2011) emphasized the need for confidential delivery of HIV prevention-related information in prisons to reduce stigma and safety threats. Timely updates on HIV prevention and care should be provided in a manner that protects individuals' HIV status. 20. Pant Pai N et al. (2009) demonstrated that continuous ART therapy in jail improved CD4 cell counts and viral load control compared to intermittent or no ART. However, inmates on intermittent ART experienced slower CD4 cell loss compared to those never on ART. 21. Evidence from 2007 showed that needle and syringe exchange programs (NSPs) in prisons are feasible and effective in reducing needle-sharing and HIV transmission. NSPs also reduce overdose risk, decrease abscesses, and facilitate referrals to drug dependence treatment programs. 22. Milloy MJ et al. (2013) found that viral loads increased during incarceration among people who inject drugs (PWID) due to treatment interruptions and hesitancy to disclose HIV status. Drug use continued in jail, reinforcing the need for needle exchange programs. 23. Seal DW et al. (2008) reported that inmates often did not use HIV prevention measures when injecting drugs, supporting the need for needle exchange and education programs. 24. Moller LF et al. (2008) observed a decrease in needle-sharing from 20% to 8% after implementing a needle exchange program in two Kyrgyzstan prisons. 25. Roshanfekr P et al. (2013) found that harm reduction services, including needle exchange programs, significantly reduced drug abuse among Iranian prisoners. 26. Studies on condom distribution in prisons, such as those by Sylla M et al. (2010) and Butler T et al. (2013), showed no evidence of increased sexual activity but demonstrated increased safer sex practices.
